title: Truly subcubic APSP
formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.

progress.text: Subcubic equivalences connect APSP to min-plus products, negative triangles and several other tasks; the full manuscript distinguishes integer-range reductions from its strongly polynomial randomized reduction.
Williams obtains randomized time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) on the real RAM; STOC publishes the result in 2014 and an expanded journal version appears in 2018.
The few-weights manuscript gives deterministic improvements under restrictions on the number of outgoing weights per vertex, with explicit weight-model conventions.
ICALP publishes the matrix-multiplication-time node-weighted zero-triangle result; independently weighted edges remain a different target.
The prediction-assisted APSP preprint gives a fixed exponent saving when its supplied certificate has sufficiently few erroneous or unverifiable pairs.
The black-box-reduction preprint establishes barriers for reductions uniform over arbitrary triangle relations; it does not establish an unrestricted APSP lower bound.

status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The published July 2026 node-weighted-triangle introduction and July prediction-assisted APSP preprint explicitly retain the general fixed-exponent challenge. The inspected few-weight algorithms, extra-prediction bounds and August black-box reduction barriers do not resolve the uniform randomized comparison-addition real-RAM question stated here. Bounded current searches located no full matching solution claim. This is an individual formulation and source-scope review, not exhaustive certification of every cited proof or all later literature.

context_blocks.text: If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

sentences: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary exact real edge weights and no negative cycle, and the output gives the shortest distance for every ordered vertex pair.
The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a fixed positive saving below the cubic exponent, correct on the entire output matrix with probability at least two thirds.
Time is charged in a specified comparison-addition real RAM that also permits ordinary logarithmic-size word operations, including all preprocessing and output.
Known general algorithms achieve subpolynomial savings, while faster restricted results concern node weights, few outgoing weights, or supplied predictions.
Recent restrictions on black-box reductions do not rule out all APSP algorithms, and the inspected sources retain the full target as unresolved.

source_formulation.text: This retains the existing arbitrary-real-weight randomized APSP question and its comparison-addition model with ordinary logarithmic-size word operations. It makes uniformity, primitive operations, the graph promise and joint output guarantee explicit. The cited equivalence literature also states integer-weight theorems with a logarithmic dependence on the weight range; its strongly polynomial reduction is identified separately rather than silently equating all weight and machine conventions.
